The wrapper's own function does the one thing a caller should never have to repeat: it reads the legacy object in its own vocabulary,

You pass if the wrapper implements a virtual interface, holds the legacy object by reference or pointer rather than copying it, and does the conversion once, inside itself, rather than at the call site. Converting at the call site and handing
the raw counts still runs today and is a partial pass: it repeats at every other call site tomorrow. Adding a
is a fail when that class really is a vendor's and not yours to edit.
Adapter wraps an object whose interface you cannot change so it satisfies an interface your own code already calls. The class being wrapped is the
, unchanged, often a vendor's own class; the interface your code calls is the

; the small class doing the translating is the adapter. What the adaptee computes never changes, only the shape a caller uses to reach it: a function's name, a parameter's type, a unit, or how a failure is reported.
The problem is a class that does the right thing in the wrong words. A rangefinder library that returns inches as a

, or reports a fault as -999 instead of nothing, forces every caller who reads it to repeat the same conversion and the same fault check, correctly, every time. Change the vendor, and every one of those call sites has to change with it.

The mechanism is a small class, holding a reference or pointer to an adaptee object that already exists, that implements the target interface and, inside each of its own functions, calls the matching function on that adaptee and translates the answer: converts the unit, renames the call, turns a sentinel into

, inheriting the adaptee privately and the target publicly instead of pointing at one: that only compiles when the adaptee can be derived from, it builds its own adaptee as part of itself rather than wrapping one that already exists, and it lets the adapter override one of the adaptee's own virtual functions from the inside, which holding a reference never allows.

What it costs is one indirect call and a class that exists only to translate, and it earns nothing at a single call site: a plain function that converts and returns is smaller there and equally safe. Reach for it once the target is called from several places, or held in something like a
of interfaces that mixes more than one kind of adaptee.

You meet this wherever a driver, a message type or a vendor SDK speaks a different unit or a different vocabulary from the rest of the robot, and it is the interview question itself: hold the adaptee or inherit it, and why.

Both cost the same 16 bytes here, and, built this way, neither leaves the adaptee's own interface reachable from outside either. What is left to choose on is whether the code already has an adaptee object to wrap, or is content to let the adapter build its own, and whether the adapter needs to override one of the adaptee's own virtual functions from the inside, which only inheriting from it makes possible. That is Klaus Iglberger's comparison in Guideline 24 of C++ Software Design, "Use Adapters to Standardize Interfaces": he compares the two forms alongside function adapters, small standard-library wrappers such as
that adapt a callable's shape rather than an object's, and treats the object form as the default, keeping the class form for the one case above an object adapter cannot match.

Adapter, Facade and Decorator all wrap something, and only one of the three changes what a call does.
takes one adaptee and makes it answer to an interface the caller already has, and the answer it gives is exactly what the adaptee would have given, translated.

, a pattern this course does not cover on its own, wraps one object behind the interface it already has and adds behaviour before or after forwarding the call, so several decorators can stack around the same object.

, the next topic, does not adapt any single interface at all: it stands in front of several different subsystems and offers one simpler entry point across all of them, hiding coordination rather than translating a shape. Reaching for Facade to solve an Adapter problem gives you a coordinating class in front of one object, which is a wrapper doing nothing; reaching for Adapter to solve a Facade problem gives you one class inheriting four unrelated interfaces, which still compiles: if two of them declare a function with the same name, the two meanings collapse into whatever single override that class provides, and only when the class overrides neither name does an unqualified call to it become ambiguous instead.
